questions: Run a load test of the new checkout against the payment provider's test environment at the expected sale-day order rate and its calls per order, and ask the provider in writing what rate limits and fraud rules apply to your account on sale day.
Is there a server-side feature flag that can switch the new checkout off for all app versions within minutes without a store release, and has the team tested switching it on and off in production?
Check the beta build on a set of older and low-end Android and iOS devices (the ones in your sale-week analytics top 20) and confirm the payment sheet renders and completes an order on each.

Beyond crashes, what do the beta's order logs show for checkout step drop-off, payment errors, timeouts and frozen screens compared with the current checkout? Query these directly and compare the rates.
Who was in the beta (how they joined, device types, sample size, how long it ran) and does the 8% lift hold when you compare only against a matched group of non-beta users with similar past spending?
Has the new checkout been tested with sale discount codes, bundles and promotional pricing, including the specific code path that applies stacked discounts, in a staging environment?

Ask the app store review contacts or look at your own last ten submissions: what were the actual review times (median and worst case), and does the payment-flow change trigger a special policy review? What is the latest submission date that still leaves a buffer of several days?

What share of your 2 million users are on the current app version and how fast did the last update spread, in days to reach 50 and 80 percent? Check the version-adoption chart from the previous release.

Do the deep links in the push notification work correctly in both the old and new app versions against the new backend? Tap the link on a phone with the old version installed and on one with the new version.

Put numbers on both sides: what is the expected sale-week revenue gain from the 8% lift at your normal conversion, and what is the revenue lost per hour of a checkout outage in sale week; at what outage length does shipping lose?

lean.option: Ship the new checkout before the sale
lean.reasons: The beta showed about an 8% conversion lift and the crash dashboard shows stability equal to the current build, so shipping early captures the gain for the biggest revenue week of the year.

premortem: The beta audience was mostly power users on recent phones; on older Android devices common among sale shoppers the new payment sheet fails to render, and checkout silently breaks for a large slice of users once the push notification brings in the crowd.

The payment provider's rate limits or fraud rules were never tested at sale-day volume; the new checkout makes more calls per order, and the provider throttles or flags transactions in the first hour.

App store review takes longer than expected or rejects the build for a payments-policy reason, so the update lands in the middle of the sale and users get a staged rollout where half see the old flow and support cannot reproduce complaints.
Many users do not update their app before the sale; the push notification sends them to a deep link that the old version handles differently from the new backend, producing dead links or cart errors.

The conversion lift in the beta came from an unusual segment (for example users who opted into the beta and were already high-intent), so the gain does not appear at full scale, while a rare crash tied to a specific discount-code path appears only under sale promotions.

beliefs.belief: The new checkout raises conversion by about 8% for the general user base.
beliefs.how_wrong: Beta users self-select and are not representative; the beta ran under normal trading conditions, not sale pricing and discount codes, and it may have run on a small sample.

beliefs.belief: The new build is as stable as the current one.
beliefs.rests_on: The crash dashboard comparing beta and current builds.
beliefs.how_wrong: Crash dashboards miss non-crash failures like frozen payment screens or silent order errors, and the beta had far fewer users and no sale-level load.

beliefs.belief: The app stores will approve and release the update before the sale starts.
beliefs.rests_on: Past review times and the nine-day window.
beliefs.how_wrong: Review times vary and a rejection resets the clock; a past pattern of fast approvals says little about a payment-flow change right before a holiday period.

beliefs.belief: Backend and payment systems will cope with sale-day traffic through the new checkout.
beliefs.rests_on: The team's assumption that infrastructure that handled last year's sale will handle this one.
beliefs.how_wrong: The new checkout changes call patterns and was never load-tested at sale volume, and the payment provider's limits may be different from last year.

beliefs.belief: Most of the 2 million users will be on the new version when the sale starts.
beliefs.rests_on: A general expectation that users auto-update quickly.
beliefs.how_wrong: Update adoption is gradual, and many users have auto-update off; the notification will reach people on the old version.

beliefs.belief: If something goes wrong, the team can recover quickly.
beliefs.rests_on: The team's experience handling past issues and the ability to ship a fix.
beliefs.how_wrong: Rollback needs another store release, which takes days and cannot reach users who do not update; a server-side switch may not exist for this change.

beliefs.belief: Waiting until after the sale would forfeit the lift and be the costlier option.
beliefs.rests_on: The 8% figure applied to expected sale revenue.
beliefs.how_wrong: The benefit is estimated from beta data, while the downside of an outage in the peak week was not priced in the same way.
